title: Joel: old men shall dream (Joel 3:1)
hook: the spirit poured on all: "your old men shall dream dreams"

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hosea's last chapter: return, and bring words with you. Your line was take with you words. Did the plain sorry get said? Today, the second voice on the scroll of the Twelve. Day eight hundred twenty.

Who gets to dream? The book of Joel opens with a disaster. Locusts, wave after wave, stripping the vines and the fig trees bare, until the fields mourn and the offerings stop. Joel calls for fasting, for gathering, for turning back. Rend your heart, he says, and not your garments. And then, after the ruin and the return, a promise comes that has nothing to do with crops. It's about who gets to see the future.
screen: `WHO GETS TO DREAM?` → `LOCUSTS STRIP THE LAND.` → `THEN A PROMISE ABOUT SEEING.`

segments.voice: In the King James words: "I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions." All flesh. Then the text goes out of its way to name who that includes. Sons and daughters. The old and the young. And in the next verse, the servants and the handmaids. Even the people at the bottom of the household are named. In Jewish Bibles this is the start of chapter three; in the King James it's the end of chapter two. Same words. And notice the old men. They aren't told to remember, or to advise, or to step aside for the young. They dream. In this promise, dreaming isn't the property of the young with their whole lives ahead. The spirit comes to the old, and what it gives them is something new to see. In the Torah, Moses hears that two men are prophesying in the camp, away from the tent where the elders gathered, and Joshua asks him to stop them. His answer, in the King James words: "would God that all the LORD's people were prophets." Joel's promise reads like that wish coming true. Not one prophet on a mountain. A whole people, any age, any rank, with the spirit poured out like rain on a field the locusts left bare. Joel doesn't say what the old men will dream. Only that they will.
screen: `UPON ALL FLESH.` · `SONS, DAUGHTERS, SERVANTS, HANDMAIDS.` · then, large: `YOUR OLD MEN SHALL DREAM DREAMS.` · then: `WOULD GOD THAT ALL WERE PROPHETS.`

segments.voice: The practice: dream something, at any age. Let your shoulders drop, and breathe. Whatever age you are, there may be a voice somewhere that says it's too late, or too early, or not for someone like you. Set it down for two minutes. Let one dream come. It doesn't have to be grand: a skill, a trip, a kindness, a thing you'd like to build or mend. Don't plan it. Just let yourself see it, the way Joel promises the old will dream. If you pray, you can hold it before God. The bell holds the time.
Joel. The prophet of the locusts, who promises a spirit poured out on all flesh, so that even the old dream dreams. Today's word.
Your line: old men dream dreams. Today, ask someone older than you what they still dream about, and really listen to the answer. Day eight hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Joel is one of the Twelve in the Hebrew Bible; Jews read Joel 2 as part of the haftarah on Shabbat Shuvah in some communities, alongside Hosea 14.
